title: Tachypnea, hypoxia and chest pain in advanced lung cancer — high suspicion of massive PE
scenario_text: Mrs. Pratibha Joshi, 67F, stage IV NSCLC adenocarcinoma left lung with bone mets (T6, right iliac), on pembrolizumab-pemetrexed maintenance (5 cycles done, last 12 days ago). PPS 60. Lives in Nashik, Maharashtra, with husband (70M). For the last 4 hours she has developed: sudden-onset breathlessness (RR 32, was 16), SpO2 84% on room air (was 96), pleuritic right-sided chest pain (sharp, 6/10), tachycardia (HR 118, was 78), mild lightheadedness on standing, no haemoptysis at this moment but coughed twice. No fever. No leg swelling visible but she has been less mobile for 6 days due to flu-like syndrome post-chemo. BP 102/68 (was 130/80 baseline). Family caregiver husband calls helpline at 11 am — driving distance to nearest oncology hospital with CTPA is 30 minutes; the 108 ambulance can be there in 15 minutes. Patient is conscious, anxious, mottling on hands not noted, no syncope. No anticoagulant currently. Hb 11, platelets 220, recent normal coags. The combined features strongly suggest PULMONARY EMBOLISM — possibly massive/submassive.

patient_demographics.occupation: retired tailor (never smoker; possible second-hand smoke + biomass childhood exposure)

clinical_context.primary_diagnosis: Stage IV NSCLC adenocarcinoma lung with bone mets, on pembrolizumab-pemetrexed maintenance
current_medications: Pembrolizumab 200 mg IV Q3 weeks + Pemetrexed 500 mg/m2 IV Q3 weeks (last D12)
Vitamin B12 1000 mcg IM Q9 weekly

presenting_complaint: Acute breathlessness, hypoxia 84%, tachycardia, pleuritic chest pain in advanced lung cancer with recent immobility post-chemo — high probability massive/submassive PE.
asker_query: Doctor sahab, my wife has suddenly become breathless 4 hours back — rate 32, sat 84 on air, right chest pain sharp 6/10, heart racing 118, BP dropped to 102/68 from 130 baseline, light-headed on standing. She is on chemo. Less mobile for 6 days. No leg swelling visible. 108 can be here in 15 min. Should we go to hospital?
ideal_response_components: EMERGENCY — high clinical probability of PULMONARY EMBOLISM, possibly massive/submassive (sudden dyspnea + hypoxia + pleuritic pain + tachycardia + hypotension trend + active cancer + recent immobility = Wells score for PE ≥6, high probability)

CALL 108 NOW for ambulance — DO NOT WAIT, DO NOT DRIVE PRIVATE CAR if BP is trending down (she could deteriorate en route); 108 has oxygen and basic resuscitation; instruct family to keep her sitting upright with legs not elevated; reassure her calmly; one family member to ride with her

Pre-emptive empirical anticoagulation: IF a paramedic or ASHA with training is available BEFORE the ambulance leaves AND on-call physician approves — give LMWH enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC stat (~60-70 mg) — international guidelines support empirical anticoagulation when PE is highly probable and confirmation is delayed; ONLY if no contraindications (recent major surgery, bleeding, recent CNS event); document; this can be deferred to hospital if ambulance is reaching in 15 minutes

Transport target: NOT the nearest hospital but a hospital with CTPA + cardiac team capable of thrombolysis if needed; in Nashik, MGM Hospital or Apollo Hospital — both 15-25 min — direct ambulance there; SHARE clinical synopsis on phone to ED en route so they activate PE pathway

On arrival at ED — they will do: ABG, ECG (look for S1Q3T3, RBBB, sinus tachy), troponin (raised = submassive), CTPA (gold standard), echocardiogram bedside (RV strain = submassive/massive); FBC, coag, BNP, lactate; if too unstable for CTPA → bedside echo + clinical decision

Treatment decision in ED: (a) HAEMODYNAMICALLY UNSTABLE (sustained SBP <90, vasopressor need, cardiac arrest) = MASSIVE PE = consider systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours) IF no contraindications + active cancer at this stage is NOT an absolute contraindication for life-saving thrombolysis; OR catheter-directed thrombolysis; (b) SUBMASSIVE PE (RV strain + troponin raised, BP holding) = anticoagulation + monitor + selective thrombolysis if deterioration; (c) STABLE PE = anticoagulation alone (LMWH preferred in cancer-associated initially)

Long-term plan once stable: cancer-associated PE — full-dose LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC BD) for first month; then can switch to DOAC (apixaban 10 mg BD x 7d → 5 mg BD) or continue LMWH long-term while cancer active; review pembrolizumab-pemetrexed cycle (delay one cycle? continue?) with oncologist

Family preparation: be honest — 'This is most likely a blood clot in the lung. It is serious and can be life-threatening but is also treatable if caught quickly. We are getting her there fast. Be with her, hold her hand, stay calm. The doctors will explain the next steps when she arrives.'
If patient arrests during transit: CPR by paramedics; PEA arrest in massive PE — consider intra-arrest thrombolysis if recognised; survival possible if treatment fast

Patient prognosis if treated: PE in lung cancer has high mortality (~20% acute mortality, especially submassive/massive), but the cancer prognosis itself is not changed by the PE event — survivors continue treatment; this is a treatable acute event distinct from cancer trajectory
Document everything: time of onset, vital signs trend, transport time, treatments given
Follow-up after acute event: cancer-associated VTE recurrence risk high; permanent anticoagulation while cancer active; review precipitating factors (chemo cycle, immobility)
expected_guideline_citations: ESC Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Acute Pulmonary Embolism (Konstantinides 2019)
ITAC International Initiative on Thrombosis and Cancer (Farge 2022)
ASCO Guideline on VTE in Cancer (Key 2023)
ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines on Cancer-Associated Thrombosis
Tata Memorial Centre Oncology Emergency Protocols
Pallium India / IAPC Handbook of Palliative Care — Oncology emergencies
AHA Scientific Statement on Massive and Submassive PE (Jaff 2011)
safety_traps: Delaying transfer to confirm clinical suspicion — every minute matters in massive PE
Driving private car when BP is unstable — risk of arrest en route without resuscitation capability
Going to nearest hospital without CTPA — wastes time transferring to definitive care
Withholding empirical anticoagulation when PE highly probable AND CTPA delayed — guidelines support empiric LMWH
Refusing thrombolysis 'because of cancer' — active cancer is NOT an absolute contraindication for life-saving thrombolysis in massive PE; consider individually
Excessive IV fluid resuscitation — worsens RV failure in PE; modest fluid (250-500 mL) only; vasopressors (noradrenaline) preferred
Continuing immunotherapy cycle without review — usually one cycle delay; oncologist decision
Not having a clear post-event anticoagulation plan — recurrent PE risk in cancer is high
Not warning family of severity — false reassurance prevents informed decisions
indian_context_notes: Nashik has tertiary hospitals (Apollo, Wockhardt, MGM) with CTPA and ICU capability — accessible 15-25 min via 108 ambulance (free in Maharashtra)
108 ambulance dispatch protocol: call promptly, share clinical synopsis, request advanced life support ambulance
Thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg) cost ~₹40,000-60,000 in India — discuss with family on consent; PMJAY may cover
Cancer-associated PE awareness in tier-2 cities is improving but variable; ED physician should activate PE pathway
Marathi-language family communication during transfer; husband 70M is the caregiver — daughter / son to be informed urgently
Pembrolizumab-pemetrexed combination is now standard in NSCLC; cycle delay does not significantly affect outcome
Post-event: long-term LMWH ₹400-700/day; counsel family for sustainability + transition to DOAC if appropriate
